placeholders.name: PRODUCT NAME
placeholders.what: The exact product name as it will appear on your store listing or ad. Use the actual title you sell under, not a generic category name, so the description reads specifically about this item.
examples: Lodge 10.25-inch Pre-Seasoned Cast Iron Skillet
Bluetooth Noise-Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones — Model AH-200
Organic Cotton Waffle-Knit Bath Towel Set (4-Piece)

placeholders.name: PASTE SPECS: materials, dimensions, weight, what it does, what's included, certifications/test results
placeholders.what: Every real, verifiable fact about the product you're willing to have quoted back in the description. The AI is told to use ONLY this list, so anything you leave out won't appear, and anything false you include will end up in the copy. Pull this from your actual spec sheet or manufacturer documentation, not memory.
examples: Material: cast iron, pre-seasoned with 3 layers of vegetable oil. Diameter: 10.25". Weight: 5.2 lbs. Oven-safe to 500°F. Includes: skillet only, no lid. Certification: none.
Material: 100% recycled aluminum shell, silicone ear cushions. Battery: 30-hour playback, USB-C charging. Weight: 250g. Includes: charging cable, carrying pouch, 2 ear tip sizes. Bluetooth 5.3.
Material: 100% GOTS-certified organic cotton, 500 GSM. Set includes: 1 bath towel (30x56"), 2 hand towels (16x28"), 1 washcloth. Machine washable, cold water. OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified.

placeholders.name: WHO IS BUYING THIS, e.g. "home cooks who are tired of pans warping on high heat"
placeholders.what: One specific real buyer and the one problem they're solving when they land on this page — this is who the description should open by speaking to. Naming a vague audience produces vague copy; naming a specific frustration produces copy that hooks people.
examples: Home cooks who are tired of nonstick pans warping or peeling after a year of daily use
Remote workers who need noise-cancelling headphones for video calls in a noisy shared apartment
New parents buying their first set of towels for a nursery who want something soft but durable through frequent washing

placeholders.name: LIST 2-3 FACTS
placeholders.what: Concrete, factual differences between your product and typical competitors — not adjectives like "better quality," but things you can point to (a warranty, a process, a test result). These become the backbone of why a shopper should pick you.
examples: Triple-seasoned in the factory vs. single-coat competitors; lifetime warranty against warping; made in a foundry operating since 1896
30-hour battery vs. the 20-hour industry average; shell made from recycled aluminum vs. virgin plastic; 2-year warranty vs. the standard 1-year
GOTS-certified organic cotton vs. unlabeled "cotton blend" competitors; 500 GSM density vs. the common 400 GSM; OEKO-TEX certified free of harmful chemicals

placeholders.name: LENGTH, e.g. 120-160 words
placeholders.what: How long you want the main description paragraph to be, separate from the bullet list. Pick a length that matches where it will be published — shorter for a mobile-first marketplace listing, longer for a dedicated product page.
examples: 120-160 words
80-100 words for a mobile-first marketplace listing
200-250 words for a dedicated brand product page

placeholders.name: e.g. "warm and direct, like a knowledgeable friend, not a hype ad"
placeholders.what: How the description should sound — match this to your brand's actual voice elsewhere (your emails, your Instagram captions) so the page doesn't sound like it was written by someone else. Be specific rather than just saying "professional."
examples: Warm and direct, like a knowledgeable friend, not a hype ad
Confident and minimal, short sentences, no exclamation points
Playful and a little cheeky, like talking to a friend who already loves the brand

variations.label: Short version for a marketplace listing
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the description is going on Amazon, Etsy, or another marketplace with strict character limits and shoppers skimming fast on their phone.
variations.prompt:
Write a short product description for [PRODUCT NAME] for a marketplace listing (Amazon/Etsy style), that will sell it honestly.

Facts about the product (use ONLY these — do not invent materials, results, or claims not listed):
[PASTE SPECS: materials, dimensions, weight, what it does, what's included, certifications/test results]

Buyer: [WHO IS BUYING THIS]
Real differentiators vs typical alternatives: [LIST 2-3 FACTS]

Requirements:
- 60-90 words maximum, plus a 5-bullet feature list (each bullet under 12 words).
- Lead with the buyer's problem in the first sentence.
- Every benefit claim must trace directly to a fact I gave you — if you want to add a claim I didn't support, put it in a separate "needs a source" list instead.
- No unverifiable superlatives ("best," "revolutionary," "clinically proven") — marketplace policies can suspend listings for these.
- Tone: [e.g. "warm and direct, like a knowledgeable friend"].

variations.label: Longer brand-story version for your own product page
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're writing for your own Shopify or website product page where you have more room and want to weave in real brand story details instead of just facts and bullets.
variations.prompt:
Write a longer product description for [PRODUCT NAME] for our own website product page, that will sell it honestly.

Facts about the product (use ONLY these): [PASTE SPECS]
Buyer: [WHO IS BUYING THIS]
Real differentiators vs typical alternatives: [LIST 2-3 FACTS]
Real brand story detail worth including (only if true): [e.g. "handmade in small batches by a 3-person team in Portland"]

Requirements:
- 200-250 words, structured as: opening hook on the buyer's problem, 2-3 short paragraphs weaving in the facts and brand story, then a 5-bullet feature list.
- Every benefit claim must trace to a fact I gave you; anything else goes in a separate "needs a source" list.
- No unverifiable superlatives unless I gave you data supporting it.
- Tone: [e.g. "warm and direct, like a knowledgeable friend, not a hype ad"].

variations.label: Rewriting an existing description you already have
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you already have a live description that's underperforming or full of vague hype, and want it rebuilt from real facts instead of starting from a blank page.
variations.prompt:
Here is our current live product description for [PRODUCT NAME], which I think is too vague/hype-y and want rewritten to be honest and specific:

[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

Real facts about the product (use ONLY these to rewrite — flag and remove any claim in the current version that isn't backed by one of these facts): [PASTE SPECS]
Buyer: [WHO IS BUYING THIS]
Real differentiators: [LIST 2-3 FACTS]

Rewrite it to: lead with the buyer's problem, keep every claim traceable to a fact above, cut any claim from the old version that isn't supported (list those separately as "removed — unverifiable"), and match this tone: [e.g. "warm and direct"]. Keep it to [LENGTH].

followUps.label: Check it didn't invent anything
followUps.prompt: Go through your draft line by line and list every claim or benefit stated. For each one, quote the exact fact from my input list that supports it. If any claim doesn't trace to something I gave you, flag it and move it to the "needs a source" list instead of leaving it in the main copy.

followUps.label: Too generic? Make the opening more specific
followUps.prompt: The opening line still sounds like it could describe any product in this category. Rewrite just the first sentence to name the buyer's specific frustration in concrete terms, not a general benefit statement.

followUps.label: Cut it down
followUps.prompt: This is too long. Cut it to [X] words without losing any of the factual claims — tighten sentences rather than deleting whole ideas, and keep the 5-bullet list intact.

followUps.label: Make the bullets scannable
followUps.prompt: Rewrite the 5 bullets so each one leads with the concrete benefit in the first 3-4 words, not the feature name — someone skimming should understand the payoff without reading the whole bullet.

ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.walkthrough:
Priya runs a small kitchenware store on Shopify and needs a description for a cast iron skillet she recently started stocking. She opens the spec sheet the manufacturer sent her, a PDF with diameter, weight, seasoning process, and oven-safe temperature, and keeps it open in a second tab.

She opens Claude, pastes the lesson's prompt, and fills in the blanks: PRODUCT NAME becomes "Lodge 10.25-inch Pre-Seasoned Cast Iron Skillet," the specs field becomes five lines copied straight from the PDF, WHO IS BUYING THIS becomes "home cooks tired of nonstick pans warping," the differentiators become the triple-seasoning process and the lifetime warranty, LENGTH becomes "120-160 words," and tone becomes "warm and direct, like a knowledgeable friend."

The AI returns a description opening with the frustration of pans that warp and stick after a year, two short paragraphs describing the seasoning process and oven-safe range in plain language, a 5-bullet list covering size, weight, oven temperature, warranty, and what's included, and a separate note: "needs a source — I wanted to say 'a kitchen staple for generations' but nothing you gave me supports that claim."

Priya reads it and notices the second paragraph runs long, so she sends the follow-up: "Cut it to 140 words without losing any of the factual claims — tighten sentences rather than deleting whole ideas." The AI trims it down, keeping every fact intact.

She checks the trimmed version against the spec sheet one more time, deletes the flagged "generations" line entirely since she can't back it up, and pastes the final copy into her Shopify product page.

Total time: about 12 minutes, most of it spent gathering the real specs before opening the AI tool at all.

placeholders.name: NUMBER, e.g. 6
placeholders.what: How many ad variants you want generated in this batch — this should match the number of angles you list below, since the prompt asks for exactly one variant per angle.

placeholders.name: PRODUCT/OFFER
placeholders.what: The specific product or promotion this ad batch is for — name it precisely so the copy doesn't drift into generic brand messaging.
examples: Eco-packaging skincare gift set ($38)
Buy-one-get-one-50%-off on all running shoes through Sunday
New arrival: waterproof commuter backpack

placeholders.name: PLATFORM, e.g. Meta feed ad
placeholders.what: Where this ad will actually run — this determines format conventions and character limits, so name the specific placement, not just "social media."
examples: Meta feed ad
Google Responsive Search Ad (RSA)
TikTok in-feed video ad caption

placeholders.name: PRICE, PROMO, KEY FEATURES, SHIPPING/RETURN TERMS
placeholders.what: The real, current offer details — price, any active promo, the actual key features, and your real shipping/return terms. This is the guardrail data that keeps the AI from inventing claims.
examples: $38, free shipping over $35, 30-day returns, key features: reef-safe ingredients, recyclable packaging
$89 (20% off $111 with code SUMMER20 through Aug 31), free 2-day shipping, 60-day returns, waterproof upper, lifetime lace guarantee
$64, no current promo, standard 5-7 day shipping, 14-day returns, TSA-approved lock, 22L capacity

placeholders.name: WHO, e.g. "first-time buyers who abandoned a cart in the last 7 days"
placeholders.what: The specific audience this ad set is targeting, matching the actual audience/retargeting segment you'll load it into.
examples: First-time buyers who abandoned a cart in the last 7 days
Existing customers who bought once 6+ months ago and haven't returned
Cold audience who has never visited the site, interested in sustainable home goods

placeholders.name: e.g. "primary text 125 chars, headline 40 chars"
placeholders.what: The exact character or word limits for the ad format and placement you chose, so the copy fits without being cut off or rejected at upload.
examples: Primary text 125 characters, headline 40 characters (Meta feed)
Headlines 30 characters each up to 15, descriptions 90 characters each up to 4 (Google RSA)
Caption 150 characters, minimal on-screen text (TikTok in-feed)

placeholders.name: ANGLE 1, e.g. Price/value
placeholders.what: The distinct angle or hypothesis you want that variant to test — this repeats for angles 1 through 6 in the prompt. Pick angles that are genuinely different core messages, not six ways of saying the same thing.
examples: 1. Price/value 2. Social proof ("2,400+ five-star reviews") 3. Urgency/scarcity ("only 40 left in this size") 4. Problem → solution (dry, irritated skin) 5. Feature-led (reef-safe, recyclable ingredients) 6. Lifestyle/aspirational (a self-care evening routine)
1. Price/value (BOGO 50% off) 2. Social proof 3. Urgency (sale ends Sunday) 4. Problem → solution (uncomfortable running shoes)
1. Feature-led (waterproof, TSA lock) 2. Lifestyle (weekend commuter) 3. Social proof 4. Urgency (back-to-school stock limited)

variations.label: Fewer, higher-budget variants for a small test budget
variations.whenToUse: Use this when your ad budget or audience size is too small to properly test 6 variants at once — fewer variants with more spend each gives you a real read faster.
variations.prompt:
Write 3 ad copy variants for [PRODUCT/OFFER] on [PLATFORM].

Offer facts (use only these): [PRICE, PROMO, KEY FEATURES, SHIPPING/RETURN TERMS]
Audience: [WHO]
Character limits: [LIMITS]

My budget/audience size is small, so I only want to test 3 genuinely different angles at once instead of 6:
1. [ANGLE 1]
2. [ANGLE 2]
3. [ANGLE 3]

For each: label the angle, give the headline + primary text, stay within character limits, and do not add a claim, discount, or guarantee I didn't list above.

variations.label: Google Search ad version (headlines + descriptions)
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the destination is Google RSA instead of a social feed ad — the format is short headline fragments, not a paragraph of primary text.
variations.prompt:
Write [NUMBER] ad variants for [PRODUCT/OFFER] as Google Responsive Search Ad (RSA) assets.

Offer facts (use only these): [PRICE, PROMO, KEY FEATURES, SHIPPING/RETURN TERMS]
Audience: [WHO]
Format: up to 15 headlines (30 characters each) and up to 4 descriptions (90 characters each), pulling from these angles — write headline/description pairs per angle:
1. [ANGLE 1]
2. [ANGLE 2]
3. [ANGLE 3]
4. [ANGLE 4]

Keep every headline and description within the character limit exactly (count characters, don't estimate), label which angle each belongs to, and do not add a claim, discount, or guarantee I didn't list above.

variations.label: Iterating on the winning angle after a test
variations.whenToUse: Use this after a test has already declared a winning angle, to generate new variants that push deeper on that one angle instead of testing new ones.
variations.prompt:
Our last A/B test found that the [WINNING ANGLE, e.g. "urgency/scarcity"] angle outperformed the others for [PRODUCT/OFFER] on [PLATFORM]. Write 4 new variants that all stay within that same angle but test different specific executions of it (different trigger, different phrasing, different framing) — not a return to generic copy.

Offer facts (use only these): [PRICE, PROMO, KEY FEATURES, SHIPPING/RETURN TERMS]
Audience: [WHO]
Character limits: [LIMITS]

Label each variant with what specific execution of the angle it's testing, and do not add a claim, discount, or guarantee I didn't list above.

followUps.label: Check the angles are actually different
followUps.prompt: Read back the core message of each variant in one sentence per variant. If any two variants have essentially the same core message despite different wording, tell me which ones and replace one of them with a genuinely different angle.

followUps.label: Check it didn't invent an offer
followUps.prompt: List every price, discount percentage, guarantee, and claim mentioned across all variants. For each one, confirm it matches exactly what I gave you in the offer facts, and flag anything that doesn't.

followUps.label: Verify character limits
followUps.prompt: Go through each variant and give me the exact character count for the headline and primary text. Flag any that exceed the limit I gave you and shorten just those.

followUps.label: Sounds too much like an ad? Make one variant more native
followUps.prompt: Take variant [NUMBER] and rewrite it to sound less like a traditional ad and more like an organic post or a friend's recommendation — same angle and offer facts, just less salesy phrasing.

ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.walkthrough:
Marcus sells eco-packaging skincare sets and wants to test ad copy before boosting a Meta campaign for cart abandoners. He opens Meta Ads Manager in one tab to check his current character limits, and a note with his real offer, $38, free shipping over $35, 30-day returns, in another.

He pastes the lesson's prompt into ChatGPT and fills in: NUMBER is 6, PRODUCT/OFFER is the skincare set, PLATFORM is Meta feed ad, the offer facts and audience (cart abandoners in the last 7 days) go in as written, character limits are 125/40, and he lists six angles: price/value, social proof, urgency, problem-solution, feature-led, lifestyle.

The AI returns six labeled variants. Reading through them, Marcus notices the "urgency" and "lifestyle" variants both lean on the same "treat yourself this weekend" framing, different words, same idea. He sends the follow-up: "Read back the core message of each variant in one sentence per variant. If any two variants have essentially the same core message, tell me which ones and replace one with a genuinely different angle."

The AI flags the overlap and rewrites the lifestyle variant around a self-care evening routine instead, which reads as a clearly different angle from urgency around stock.

Marcus double-checks the character counts against Meta's limits, confirms no invented discount snuck in, and loads four of the six variants into his test, naming each ad by its angle so he can trace results later.

Total time: about 15 minutes.

placeholders.name: PRODUCT
placeholders.what: The name of the real product you're generating a scene around. This should match your actual product exactly since the goal is placing the real item into a new setting, not designing a new one.
examples: Ceramic pour-over coffee mug, terracotta glaze
Waterproof canvas commuter backpack, olive green
10oz soy candle, "Cedar & Fog" scent, amber glass jar

placeholders.name: PLATFORM/PLACEMENT, e.g. "Instagram feed ad background" — NOT a marketplace primary listing photo
placeholders.what: Exactly where this image will be used — this determines aspect ratio, composition, and whether AI generation is even appropriate. Never put this in a marketplace's primary listing photo slot.
examples: Instagram feed ad background
Seasonal homepage banner for the website
Email newsletter header image

placeholders.name: SETTING, e.g. "sunlit kitchen counter, morning"
placeholders.what: The physical scene or backdrop you want around the product — be specific about location, time of day, and any props, since vague settings produce generic stock-photo-style results.
examples: Sunlit kitchen counter, morning, small potted herb plant blurred in background
Weathered wooden park bench, golden hour, autumn leaves scattered nearby
Minimalist marble bathroom shelf, soft diffused daylight

placeholders.name: COMPOSITION, e.g. "product on left third, negative space right for text overlay"
placeholders.what: Where the product should sit in the frame and how much empty space to leave — plan this around where you'll add text or a logo afterward.
examples: Product on left third, negative space right for text overlay
Product centered, symmetrical framing, no room needed for text
Product in lower third, most of frame is open sky for a banner headline

placeholders.name: LIGHTING
placeholders.what: The light quality and direction you want — this has a huge effect on mood and on whether the scene matches your other product photography.
examples: Soft natural window light from the left, warm tone
Bright even studio lighting, no harsh shadows
Golden hour backlighting with a soft lens flare

placeholders.name: STYLE, e.g. "photorealistic, editorial food photography"
placeholders.what: The overall visual style or photographic genre to aim for — naming a real reference style gives the model a concrete target instead of a vague "nice photo."
examples: Photorealistic, editorial food photography
Clean product-catalog style, minimal shadows, studio look
35mm film photography, slightly grainy, warm tones

placeholders.name: MOOD/PALETTE matching brand colors: LIST HEX/DESCRIPTION
placeholders.what: The color palette and overall feeling that should match your existing brand materials — list actual hex codes if you have brand guidelines, or plain descriptions if you don't.
examples: Warm terracotta (#C97C4F) and cream (#F5EDE1), cozy and inviting
Cool sage green (#8FA787) and off-white, calm and minimal
Deep navy (#1B2A41) and brass accents, moody and premium

placeholders.name: ASPECT RATIO for platform
placeholders.what: The exact pixel dimensions or ratio required for where this image will be published — get this from the platform's current spec.
examples: 1:1 square (1080x1080px) for Instagram feed
9:16 vertical (1080x1920px) for Instagram/TikTok Stories
16:9 (1920x1080px) for a website homepage banner

placeholders.name: N
placeholders.what: How many variations you want generated in this batch, so you have real options to compare rather than accepting the first result.

variations.label: Seasonal banner batch (same product, multiple seasons)
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you want a set of seasonal variations of the same scene for the same product, to swap through the year without rebuilding the prompt each time.
variations.prompt:
Generate [N] seasonal variations of a lifestyle scene for [PRODUCT], for use as [PLATFORM/PLACEMENT] across the year.

Reference image attached = my actual product photo, unchanged.

Base scene concept: [SETTING], [COMPOSITION], [STYLE], [MOOD/PALETTE matching brand colors], [ASPECT RATIO for platform].

Generate one version per season, keeping composition and style consistent but varying: [SEASONAL ELEMENT, e.g. "lighting warmth, props (autumn leaves / spring flowers / summer citrus / winter pine), color temperature"].

Requirements:
- Keep the product itself exactly as shown in the reference in every version — do not redesign its shape, color, label, or add features it doesn't have.
- No text or logos rendered into the image.
- Label each variation by season.

variations.label: Quick single background for a fast social post
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a same-day social post when you just need one usable background fast, not a full comparison set.
variations.prompt:
Generate 1 quick styled background for [PRODUCT], for use as [PLATFORM/PLACEMENT] — I need one usable option today, not a full comparison set.

Reference image attached = my actual product photo, unchanged.

Scene: [SETTING], [COMPOSITION], [LIGHTING], [STYLE], [ASPECT RATIO for platform].

Requirements:
- Keep the product itself exactly as shown in the reference — do not redesign its shape, color, label, or add features it doesn't have.
- No text or logos rendered into the image.
- Generate 2 variations only so I can pick fast.

variations.label: Cross-check the same brief in the other tool before a paid placement
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a hero image going into a paid ad, where getting the product accuracy exactly right is worth generating the same brief in both ChatGPT and Gemini and comparing before you commit spend.
variations.prompt:
Generate a lifestyle/styled scene for [PRODUCT], for use as [PLATFORM/PLACEMENT — a paid placement, so accuracy matters more than usual].

Reference image attached = my actual product photo, unchanged.

Scene: [SETTING], [COMPOSITION], [LIGHTING], [STYLE], [MOOD/PALETTE matching brand colors: LIST HEX/DESCRIPTION], [ASPECT RATIO for platform].

Requirements:
- Keep the product itself exactly as shown in the reference — do not redesign its shape, color, label, or add features it doesn't have.
- No text or logos rendered into the image.
- Generate [N] variations so I can compare.

I'm running this identical brief in both ChatGPT (GPT Image 2) and Gemini (Nano Banana 2) — after generating, tell me which of your outputs you'd flag as least faithful to the reference photo, if any, so I can compare against the other tool's results before picking a final image.

followUps.label: Product looks altered? Flag it
followUps.prompt: Compare this generated image to my reference photo specifically for the product's shape, color, and any label or logo details. Tell me exactly what, if anything, differs from the reference so I can decide whether to regenerate or reject it.

followUps.label: Regenerate with the product unchanged
followUps.prompt: The product's [SPECIFIC DETAIL, e.g. color/proportions/label] doesn't match my reference photo. Regenerate keeping the scene the same but the product exactly as shown in the reference, with no redesign.

followUps.label: Doesn't match brand colors — adjust
followUps.prompt: The color palette in this generation doesn't match our brand colors [RESTATE HEX/DESCRIPTION]. Regenerate the same scene and composition with the color grading adjusted to match.

followUps.label: Text or logo got rendered in — remove it
followUps.prompt: This generation has text/a logo rendered directly into the image, which I need removed since I'll add real text separately. Regenerate the same scene with no text or logo elements anywhere in the image.

ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.walkthrough:
Elena sells ceramic mugs and wants a cozy autumn background for an Instagram ad, without paying for a photo shoot. She takes a clean photo of her actual terracotta mug on a white background and saves it as a file she can upload.

She opens Gemini and starts a new chat, uploading that photo as a reference. She pastes the lesson's prompt, filling in PRODUCT as "ceramic pour-over mug, terracotta glaze," PLATFORM/PLACEMENT as "Instagram feed ad background," SETTING as "sunlit kitchen counter, morning, autumn leaves blurred in background," COMPOSITION as "product on left third, negative space right for text," STYLE as "photorealistic, editorial," MOOD/PALETTE as her brand's warm terracotta and cream hex codes, ASPECT RATIO as 1:1, and N as 4.

Nano Banana 2 returns four variations. In two of them, the mug's glaze reads a slightly different orange-red than her real product. She sends the follow-up: "Compare this generated image to my reference photo specifically for the product's shape, color, and any label or logo details. Tell me exactly what, if anything, differs."

Gemini flags the color shift on those two. Elena discards them and keeps the two where the mug matches her reference exactly, picking the one with the better negative space for her ad text. She asks it, in the same chat, to warm up the lighting slightly on her favorite — a quick conversational edit rather than a new prompt.

She adds her headline text separately in a design tool, since the AI was told not to render text into the image, and uploads the finished ad background.

Total time: about 18 minutes.

placeholders.name: SITUATION: refund request / shipping delay / complaint about damaged or wrong item
placeholders.what: Which of the three common situations this reply is for — this shapes the whole structure of the response, so pick the one that actually matches.
examples: Refund request
Shipping delay
Complaint about damaged or wrong item

placeholders.name: PASTE OR SUMMARIZE
placeholders.what: The customer's actual message, pasted in full if short, or summarized accurately if long or rambling. Keep their real tone and specific complaint intact. Replace any information you wouldn't want stored in a shared or logged AI tool, like their full name or email, with a placeholder if required.
examples: "This is the third email I've sent about my order and no one has responded. I ordered a birthday gift and it still hasn't shipped 9 days later. I want a refund now."
Summary: customer received the wrong item (ordered a size M jacket, got a size S), attached a photo, first contact, polite but clearly frustrated, wants a replacement in the correct size.
"My package tracking shows it's been stuck at a distribution hub for 6 days with no movement. I need this by Friday for a trip — what's going on?"

placeholders.name: ORDER #, ITEM, ORDER DATE, CURRENT STATUS, TRACKING INFO IF RELEVANT
placeholders.what: The real facts of this specific order pulled from your order management system. This is what keeps the reply grounded in reality instead of a generic apology.
examples: Order #48213, Cast Iron Skillet, ordered Aug 1, status: shipped Aug 3, tracking shows arrived at regional hub Aug 6 and no movement since
Order #55902, Waterproof Backpack (size M ordered), status: delivered Aug 5, customer reports size S received instead
Order #61034, Skincare Gift Set, ordered Jul 28, status: still processing, has not shipped as of today

placeholders.name: PASTE POLICY, e.g. "refunds within 30 days of delivery, no restocking fee, replacement offered for damaged items with photo proof"
placeholders.what: Your actual, current written policy for this exact situation, copied from your real policy document, not what you remember it being. This is the single most important guardrail in the prompt.
examples: Refunds within 30 days of delivery, no restocking fee, replacement offered for damaged items with photo proof within 14 days of delivery
For delays over 7 business days with no tracking movement, we offer either a refund of shipping cost or $10 store credit, customer's choice
Wrong item shipped: we cover return shipping and send the correct item immediately without waiting for the wrong item to be returned first

placeholders.name: WORD COUNT
placeholders.what: How long the reply should be — keep this short for a first-contact reply and slightly longer only if there's real detail to walk through.
examples: 120 words
150 words
80 words

placeholders.name: firm / apologetic / neutral — pick what fits
placeholders.what: The emotional register of the reply, chosen to match the real situation — apologetic when your company made a genuine error, neutral for a standard policy outcome, firm when the answer is no.
examples: Apologetic — we shipped the wrong item, this is our error
Neutral — explaining a standard delay that's outside our control, tracking shows it's moving
Firm — the return window has closed and no exception applies

variations.label: Angry, repeat-contact customer (third email on the same issue)
variations.whenToUse: Use when this isn't the customer's first message about the issue and they're clearly frustrated by lack of response — the reply needs to acknowledge that history.
variations.prompt:
Draft a reply to a customer email about [SITUATION]. This is their [NUMBER, e.g. "third"] email about the same issue with no prior response from us — the reply needs to acknowledge that directly, not read like a first-contact message.

Customer's message(s) (or summary, including that this is a repeat contact): [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE]
Order facts: [ORDER #, ITEM, ORDER DATE, CURRENT STATUS, TRACKING INFO IF RELEVANT]
Our actual policy for this situation: [PASTE POLICY]

Requirements:
- Open by acknowledging both the specific issue AND that this is a repeat contact with no response yet — take real ownership of the delay in responding.
- State only commitments directly supported by the policy and facts I gave you — do not invent a resolution I didn't authorize.
- If the right resolution isn't clear from what I gave you, say so and list what you need from me.
- Keep it under [WORD COUNT], warm but professional, no corporate filler.
- Tone: apologetic for the response delay, but factually firm on any policy limit that applies.

variations.label: Good news reply — refund or replacement already approved
variations.whenToUse: Use when the resolution is already decided and good, and you just need to communicate it clearly and warmly.
variations.prompt:
Draft a reply to a customer confirming a resolution that's already been approved for [SITUATION].

ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.walkthrough:
Devon runs support for a small home-goods store and gets an email from a customer whose order has been stuck at a shipping hub for 6 days. He opens the order in Shopify to check the real facts: order #48213, cast iron skillet, ordered August 1, tracking shows no movement since August 6. He also has the store's written delay policy open in a doc: refund of shipping cost or $10 store credit for delays over 7 business days.

He opens Claude and pastes the lesson's prompt, filling in SITUATION as shipping delay, the customer's actual message about needing the item by Friday for a trip, the order facts, the policy text, WORD COUNT as 120, and tone as neutral since this is a standard delay, not a company error.

The AI drafts a reply acknowledging the specific 6-day stall at the hub, honestly stating the tracking status, and noting that since the delay hasn't yet crossed the 7-business-day policy threshold, no compensation applies yet, but it will automatically once it does, and Devon should follow up then.

Devon reads it and worries it sounds too neutral given the customer mentioned a Friday deadline. He sends the follow-up: "Reread the customer's message for how frustrated they actually sound... adjust the tone without changing any of the factual commitments."

The revised version acknowledges the time pressure of the trip more directly while keeping the same factual content. Devon personalizes the greeting, adds his name, and sends it from the support platform.

Total time: about 9 minutes.

ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.walkthrough:
Sana runs a small skincare store and has never built an abandoned-cart email flow beyond her platform's default template. She gathers her real inputs: her brand voice notes, casual, a little playful, no corporate jargon, her actual policy of no discounts in this flow, and her timing plan of immediate, +24h, +72h.

She opens ChatGPT, pastes the lesson's prompt, and fills in FLOW TYPE as abandoned cart, NUMBER as 3, BRAND/STORE as Willow & Sage, PRODUCT CATEGORY as natural skincare, the brand voice description, DISCOUNT/OFFER as "none, no discount," the timing, and LIST as her best-selling serum's product link.

The AI returns three emails: email 1 sent immediately reminds what's in the cart with light urgency about limited stock, no discount anywhere; email 2 at +24h adds a customer review addressing a common hesitation about scent; email 3 at +72h uses a stronger urgency angle around a restock date. Each has a distinct subject line and stated job.

Sana reads through and worries email 1 and email 3 both lean on "stock running low," which feels repetitive. She sends the follow-up: "State the specific job of each email in this flow in one sentence. If any two emails are doing essentially the same job, tell me which ones and rewrite one."

The AI confirms the overlap and rewrites email 3's angle around the customer's own routine and past purchase interest instead of stock urgency.

Sana loads all three into her email platform's automation builder, test-triggers the flow on her own account to confirm timing and links work, then turns it on.

Total time: about 20 minutes.

placeholders.name: TASK, e.g. "draft a product description and Instagram caption every time a new product is added in Shopify"

Draft a reply suggestion whenever a new 1-2 star review comes in

placeholders.name: WHAT STARTS IT, e.g. "new product created in Shopify"

New review submitted with a rating of 1 or 2 stars

placeholders.name: LIST FIELDS, e.g. "product title, price, category, spec fields, uploaded photos"

A suggested reply draft (under 100 words) flagged for human review, not auto-sent

Real inputs available: [LIST FIELDS]
Current AI output: [WHAT SHOULD BE DRAFTED]
Tool: [Claude with Cowork + MCP connectors / ChatGPT with Agent mode + Scheduled tasks]

Real inputs available: [LIST FIELDS]
Desired AI output: [WHAT SHOULD BE DRAFTED]
Tool: [Claude with Cowork + MCP connectors / ChatGPT with Agent mode + Scheduled tasks]

Help me:

followUps.label: Simplify for a first version

ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.walkthrough:
Tom runs a mid-size Shopify store and adds 5-10 new SKUs a week, each needing a product description and an Instagram caption, work he's been doing by hand every Friday. He wants to automate the drafting step while keeping a human check before anything publishes.

He decides to build this in Claude, since his Pro plan includes Cowork and he can connect Shopify through an MCP connector. He pastes the lesson's prompt into a chat, filling in TASK as drafting a description and caption whenever a new product is added, WHAT STARTS IT as "new product created in Shopify," LIST FIELDS as title, price, category, and spec fields (Tom checks Shopify and confirms these are always filled in, unlike the optional "care instructions" field which is often blank), WHAT SHOULD BE DRAFTED as a 150-word description plus one Instagram caption with 3 hashtags, and Tool as "Claude with Cowork and a Shopify MCP connector."

Claude maps the sequence: the Shopify MCP connector detects a new product → Cowork pulls the confirmed fields → an AI drafting step uses a prompt template referencing only those fields → Cowork checks in with him, showing the draft next to the original product data → Tom approves or edits directly in that check-in → only then does it save to a drafts folder for him to publish. It also flags a risk: if the spec field is ever blank, the draft would come out thin, and suggests Cowork should flag him directly instead of drafting silently when that field is empty.

Tom sends the follow-up asking it to stress-test what happens with a missing field, confirming the guard works as described. He connects the Shopify MCP connector in Claude's settings, tests the whole thing on one real new product, and watches the first two weeks of real runs closely before considering removing the approval step later.

Total time: about 40 minutes to design and connect.

placeholders.name: PASTE DRAFT
placeholders.what: Your own rough, blunt, or emotionally-charged first attempt at the reply, even if it's just a few angry bullet points to yourself. Paste that real starting point rather than nothing, since the AI is rewriting your actual draft, not starting from a blank page.
examples: "No. Policy is 30 days, it's been 41. Not our problem you didn't check."
"We already told you twice this isn't covered under warranty. Please stop asking."
"Sorry but no refunds after opening the product, that's just how it works here."

placeholders.name: e.g. "we cannot refund — the return window closed 11 days ago and the item was used"
placeholders.what: The real, unchangeable decision exactly as it stands, stated plainly to yourself first — this is the fact the AI must keep firm no matter how it softens the delivery.
examples: We cannot refund — the return window closed 11 days ago and the item was used
We cannot expedite this order — it's already in transit and can't be rerouted
We cannot waive the warranty exclusion — the damage described is from a drop, which isn't a manufacturing defect

placeholders.name: e.g. "a 15% discount on next order, or store credit" / "nothing — this is a firm no"
placeholders.what: Anything genuinely real that you're authorized to offer as a goodwill gesture, or an explicit statement that there's nothing — never let this field be vague or aspirational.
examples: A 15% discount on their next order, or store credit for the item's value
Nothing — this is a firm no, no exceptions available
We can expedite their next order for free as a goodwill gesture, but cannot change this order's outcome

placeholders.name: ONE SENTENCE
placeholders.what: What the customer is actually upset or worried about, distilled to one honest sentence — this keeps the reply focused on acknowledging their real concern instead of a generic "I understand your frustration."
examples: They feel the 30-day window wasn't clearly communicated at checkout
They're frustrated this is the second time they've had to explain the issue
They're worried they wasted money on something they can't use

placeholders.name: WORD COUNT
placeholders.what: How long the final reply should be — keep firm-no replies tight, since padding a difficult message with extra words tends to read as either over-apologizing or burying the actual answer.
examples: 100 words
80 words
130 words

The actual decision (do not soften or change this): [ACTUAL DECISION]

cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.walkthrough:
Aisha works support at an outdoor gear store and has to reply to a customer asking for a refund on a tent used on one camping trip, well outside the 30-day window. Her first instinct draft, typed fast out of frustration with a long back-and-forth thread, reads: "No. Policy is 30 days, it's been 41. Not our problem you didn't check." She knows this can't go out as written.

She opens Claude and pastes the lesson's prompt. For the draft field she pastes her blunt line above. For the actual decision she writes: "we cannot refund, the window closed 11 days ago and the tent shows signs of use." For what she can offer, she writes: "nothing, this is a firm no, no exceptions available." For the customer's core concern, she writes: "they feel the 30-day window wasn't clearly communicated at checkout." Word count: 100.

The AI returns a reply that opens by clearly stating a refund isn't possible in the first two sentences, explains the 30-day window and usage plainly, acknowledges that the timing feels frustrating without apologizing for the policy itself, and closes without inventing any workaround.

Aisha reads it once more as the customer and worries it still reads slightly cold. She sends the follow-up: "This reads as too blunt or cold. Add genuine acknowledgment of the customer's frustration without apologizing for the decision itself."

The revised version adds one warmer sentence acknowledging the disappointment. She sends it.

Total time: about 7 minutes.

[PASTE REPLY 2 — label]
...

For each: 1) convert it into a macro with placeholders in [BRACKETS], keeping original wording and tone, 2) give a short category label, 3) add a fill-in checklist, and 4) add one sentence of guidance a new agent specifically would need to know before using this macro (e.g. "only use if the order is confirmed shipped, check tracking first").

variations.label: Converting an existing FAQ doc into macros
variations.whenToUse: Use when you already have a written internal FAQ or policy doc (not ticket replies) and want to convert its answers into the same macro format.
variations.prompt:
I have an internal FAQ/policy doc with written answers to common questions (not ticket replies). I want to convert its answers into the same macro format as ticket-based macros.

[PASTE FAQ SECTION — question + our written answer]

For each Q&A: 1) rewrite it in a natural reply voice a support agent would actually send (not FAQ-page language), matching this tone: [DESCRIBE VOICE], 2) add placeholders in [BRACKETS] for anything customer-specific, 3) give a short category label, 4) add a fill-in checklist.

followUps.label: Check it preserved your real voice
followUps.prompt: Compare this macro back to my original reply sentence by sentence. Tell me anywhere the wording, tone, or structure changed from what I wrote, rather than just having placeholders swapped in.

followUps.label: Placeholders too vague — make them specific
followUps.prompt: Review the placeholders used in this macro. Replace any vague one like [DETAILS] or [INFO] with a specific one that says exactly what to fill in, like [ORDER #] or [DAYS DELAYED].

followUps.label: Test it with a real example
followUps.prompt: Fill in this macro's placeholders with this real example and show me the finished reply, so I can check it reads naturally once filled in: [PASTE REAL DETAILS]

followUps.label: Add the fill-in checklist if missing
followUps.prompt: Add a short "fill in before sending" checklist to this macro listing exactly which placeholders must be personalized before it can be sent, I don't want an agent sending it with a placeholder still in.

cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.walkthrough:
Ben leads a 4-person support team that keeps answering the same handful of questions from scratch every time, which is slow and inconsistent. He decides to build a macro library and pulls his team's 6 best real replies from the last month's tickets, a shipping delay reply, a wrong-item reply, a password reset reply, a cancellation reply, a damaged-item reply, and a subscription pause reply.

He opens ChatGPT and pastes the lesson's prompt, setting N to 6, then pastes each reply with a one-line label, like "Label: Shipping delay, first contact" followed by the actual reply text his teammate Maria sent last week.

The AI converts each into a macro: the shipping delay reply becomes a template with [CUSTOMER NAME], [ORDER #], [CURRENT TRACKING STATUS], and [DAYS DELAYED] as placeholders, wording otherwise unchanged, labeled "Shipping delay — over 5 days," with a checklist reminding the agent to confirm the actual tracking status before sending.

Ben checks one macro against the original and notices the AI smoothed out a slightly casual phrase Maria used ("no biggie") into something more formal. He sends the follow-up: "Compare this macro back to my original reply sentence by sentence. Tell me anywhere the wording, tone, or structure changed."

The AI flags the change and restores the original phrasing. Ben tests one macro by filling in a real order number and reading it as a customer would, confirms it reads naturally, then saves all six into the team's shared macro doc with a review date three months out.

Total time: about 35 minutes.

placeholders.name: PASTE CLEANED TRANSCRIPT — CUSTOMER ISSUE + HOW IT WAS RESOLVED
placeholders.what: The full resolved ticket conversation, with every customer name, email, order number, or account-specific detail already removed or swapped for a placeholder before you paste it anywhere. Include both what the customer reported and exactly how the agent resolved it.
examples: Customer: My orders keep showing as 'processing' even after I get a shipping confirmation email. Very confusing. Agent: This happens when the store's inventory sync hasn't caught up with the shipping carrier update yet, I refreshed [CUSTOMER]'s account manually and the status updated within a few minutes. Agent note: usually resolves itself within 24 hours without manual intervention.

Customer: The app crashes every time I try to upload a photo larger than a few MB. Agent: Confirmed this happens with images over 10MB on the current app version. Had [CUSTOMER] resize the photo before uploading as a workaround, which worked. Agent note: reported to engineering as a known bug, no fix timeline yet.

Customer: I can't find where to update my shipping address after placing an order. Agent: Walked [CUSTOMER] through it, orders can only have their address changed within 1 hour of placing, after that it's locked for processing. Within that window, it's under Account > Order History > Edit Address.

variations.label: Combining multiple similar tickets into one article
variations.whenToUse: Use when you have several resolved tickets about the same underlying issue with slightly different details, so the article reflects the real range of the problem.
variations.prompt:
Turn these resolved support tickets into one general knowledge-base article, they're all about the same underlying issue with slightly different specifics, and I want the article to reflect the real range of how it shows up. All customer-identifying details have already been replaced with placeholders.

Ticket 1 (cleaned): [PASTE CLEANED TRANSCRIPT]
Ticket 2 (cleaned): [PASTE CLEANED TRANSCRIPT]
Ticket 3 (cleaned, if any): [PASTE CLEANED TRANSCRIPT]

Structure the article as: 1) Title (a real search query), 2) short summary, 3) step-by-step resolution generalized across all the tickets, note if different tickets needed different steps, 4) "when this might not work" section, 5) related issues. Do not state anything as generally true that only appeared in one of the tickets, flag those under "needs verification" instead.

variations.label: Short quick-answer article for a simple issue
variations.whenToUse: Use for a simple, well-understood issue that doesn't need the full 5-section structure.
variations.prompt:
Turn this resolved ticket into a short quick-answer help article for a simple issue. All customer-identifying details have already been replaced with placeholders.

Ticket transcript (cleaned): [PASTE CLEANED TRANSCRIPT]

Give me just: 1) Title (a real search query), 2) a 2-4 sentence direct answer, 3) one "needs verification" flag if any part of the resolution might not generalize to every customer. Keep the whole thing under 100 words, this doesn't need the full multi-section structure.

variations.label: Article aimed at internal agents, not customers
variations.whenToUse: Use when the article is for your own support team's internal knowledge base rather than a public customer-facing help center.
variations.prompt:
Turn this resolved ticket into an internal knowledge-base article for our own support team, not customers. All customer-identifying details have already been replaced with placeholders.

Ticket transcript (cleaned): [PASTE CLEANED TRANSCRIPT]

Structure it as: 1) Title (how an agent would search for this internally), 2) short summary, 3) step-by-step resolution including any internal tool names, admin panel steps, or escalation paths mentioned in the ticket, 4) "when this might not work" / when to escalate instead, 5) related internal articles or macros to check. Since this is internal-only, you can include operational detail a customer-facing article would omit, but still flag anything uncertain under "needs verification" rather than stating it as settled process.

followUps.label: Check nothing customer-specific was generalized
followUps.prompt: Reread the ticket transcript and the article side by side. Point out anywhere the article states something as generally true that was actually specific to this one customer's account or situation, and move it to the "needs verification" section.

followUps.label: Make the title a real search query
followUps.prompt: Rewrite the title as the exact phrase or question a customer would actually type into a search bar or help-center search, not a description of the internal issue.

followUps.label: Simplify the steps
followUps.prompt: Rewrite the step-by-step section in shorter, simpler steps a non-technical customer could follow without help, break any step that does more than one thing into two steps.

followUps.label: Double-check for leftover PII
followUps.prompt: Scan this article one more time for anything that could identify a real customer, a name, email, order number, or account-specific detail that wasn't replaced with a placeholder. List anything you find.

cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.walkthrough:
Renata handles support for a subscription box service and recently resolved a ticket where a customer's account showed orders stuck on "processing" even after a shipping email went out. She realizes this probably happens to other customers too, and decides to turn it into a help-center article instead of explaining it from scratch every time it comes up.

She copies the ticket transcript out of her helpdesk tool into a text file and replaces the customer's name and account email with [CUSTOMER] and [EMAIL] before pasting anything into an AI tool, since her company's policy requires that.

In Claude, she pastes the lesson's prompt with the cleaned transcript: the customer's confusion, the agent's explanation that this happens when inventory sync lags behind the shipping update, the manual refresh that fixed it immediately, and a note that it usually self-resolves within 24 hours anyway.

The AI returns a structured draft: a title phrased as "why does my order still say processing after shipping," a short summary, three generalized steps (wait 24 hours, refresh the order page, contact support if it persists past 24 hours), a "when this might not work" section, and a "needs verification" flag questioning whether the manual refresh trick works for every customer or only worked because a support agent has backend access customers don't.

Renata sends that flag to her product lead, who confirms customers can't self-refresh, so she removes that step and keeps only the wait-and-contact-support path. She publishes after that check.

Total time: about 25 minutes including the verification step.

placeholders.name: PASTE THREAD OR NOTES — include error messages, timestamps, steps already tried
placeholders.what: The raw ticket thread or your own working notes on the issue, including exact error messages as they appeared, timestamps, and anything already tried to fix it. Paste this as-is rather than cleaning it up first. Replace customer names or emails with placeholders first if your tool logs or shares AI conversations.
examples: Customer reports checkout fails with error 'PAYMENT_DECLINED_502' at the final step. Started ~9:40am today. 6 similar reports since. Agent tried: had customer clear cache and retry (still fails), tried a different card (still fails). No timestamp pattern noticed yet, all reports are US customers.

App crashes on launch with error 'SIGABRT: memory pressure' after the 2.4.1 update, reported starting yesterday evening. Affects iPhone SE and iPhone 8 users specifically so far, not seen on newer models. Agent tried: had 2 customers reinstall the app, crash still occurs on first launch.

Customer's dashboard shows '$0.00' for all historical revenue reports as of this morning, was working correctly as of last night per customer. Agent tried: logging out/in (no change), checked account in admin panel and data appears present in the database, just not rendering on the customer-facing dashboard.

placeholders.name: e.g. "affecting an estimated 40+ customers since yesterday, no known workaround" / "unknown — flag as unknown"
placeholders.what: The real scope of the problem if you know it, how many customers, since when, whether there's a workaround, or an honest "unknown" if you don't. Guessing here to sound more certain than you are will mislead whoever reads the manager summary.
examples: Affecting an estimated 40+ customers since yesterday, no known workaround
Unknown — flag as unknown, only 6 reports confirmed so far but could be wider
Confirmed to affect all customers on the 2.4.1 app update on older devices (iPhone SE and 8), roughly 15% of our user base by device type, no workaround besides staying on the previous version

variations.label: Technical summary only — engineer already has context
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're escalating directly to an engineer who's already aware of the issue and just needs the technical detail, without a separate manager-facing summary.
variations.prompt:
I need to send a technical summary only to an engineer who's already aware of this issue, no manager summary needed.

Raw thread/notes: [PASTE THREAD OR NOTES — include error messages, timestamps, steps already tried]

Give me: exact error message(s) as written, steps to reproduce as far as known, what's already been tried and ruled out, environment/version details if mentioned. Do not infer a root cause or fix that wasn't stated. Flag anything needed to reproduce that isn't in the thread as "missing — need to obtain."

variations.label: Customer-facing incident update, not internal escalation
variations.whenToUse: Use during an active incident when you need a short public or customer-facing status update instead of an internal escalation summary.
variations.prompt:
I need a short customer-facing status update for an active incident, not an internal escalation summary, this may be posted publicly or sent to affected customers, so it needs to be careful and not overpromise.

Raw thread/notes (internal only, do not include specifics from this in the public version): [PASTE THREAD OR NOTES]
Known impact: [KNOWN IMPACT]

Write a 2-3 sentence customer-facing update that: states plainly what's affected in non-technical language, does not speculate on cause, does not promise a specific fix time unless I've confirmed one, and tells customers what to do if anything (retry, wait, contact support).

variations.label: Follow-up escalation update once more is known
variations.whenToUse: Use to update an escalation that's already in progress once new information has come in, without re-writing the whole thing from scratch.
variations.prompt:
This escalation is already in progress. Here's the original summary I sent: [PASTE PREVIOUS SUMMARY]

Here's what's new since then: [PASTE NEW THREAD/NOTES — new error info, what's been tried, updated impact]

Give me an updated version of both the technical and manager summaries reflecting only what's changed, don't repeat unchanged information at length, just note what's new, what's now ruled out, and whether the known impact figure has changed. Do not infer a root cause or fix that wasn't stated.

followUps.label: Check for an inferred root cause
followUps.prompt: Reread both summaries and point out anywhere a cause, fix, or explanation is stated that wasn't actually confirmed in the raw thread I gave you, even if it sounds like a reasonable guess, flag it so I can mark it as unconfirmed or remove it.

followUps.label: Check the impact numbers match exactly
followUps.prompt: Confirm the impact figures in the manager summary match exactly what I stated, not rounded up, not more confident than what I actually know. Flag any mismatch.

followUps.label: Manager summary still too technical — simplify
followUps.prompt: The manager summary still has technical language in it. Rewrite it so a non-technical manager could read it in 15 seconds and understand what's broken, how bad it is, and what's being asked of them.

followUps.label: List what's still missing to reproduce
followUps.prompt: Give me a clean bullet list of everything flagged as "missing — need to obtain" across both summaries, so I know exactly what to go collect from the customer or logs before engineering can act on this.

cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.walkthrough:
Karim works support at a software company and starts seeing a pattern: six customers in one morning report checkout failing with the same error code. He needs to escalate this to engineering fast, and his manager will also ask what's going on, so he wants both summaries from the same facts instead of writing two separate reports under pressure.

He opens his notes doc where he's been logging each report as it came in, exact error code, timestamps, the fact that clearing cache and trying a different card didn't help, and pastes the lesson's prompt into ChatGPT. For known impact, he writes: "affecting at least 6 confirmed customers since 9:40am today, likely more not yet reported, no known workaround."

The AI returns two summaries. The technical one quotes the exact error code, lists the two failed attempts to fix it, and flags that browser and specific checkout-step details weren't captured yet, marking them "missing — need to obtain." The manager summary states checkout is failing for at least 6 customers since this morning with no workaround, and requests engineering prioritize investigating.

Karim rereads the technical summary and notices a line implying the issue might be payment-processor related, something nobody actually confirmed, only his own hunch bleeding into the draft. He sends the follow-up: "Reread both summaries and point out anywhere a cause is stated that wasn't actually confirmed... flag it."

The AI catches the line and marks it as an unconfirmed hypothesis instead of stated fact. Karim sends both summaries to their respective audiences.

Total time: about 10 minutes.

placeholders.name: PASTE 4-6 REAL REPLIES
placeholders.what: Real replies your team actually sent that you and your team agree represent the tone you want, include a mix of easy and difficult situations, not just the easy wins.
examples:
Reply 1 (easy — order status): "Hi Jamie, good news, your order shipped this morning and should land by Thursday. Tracking: [link]. Let me know if you don't see movement by Wednesday."

Reply 2 (difficult — denied refund): "Hi Alex, I checked and unfortunately this falls outside our 30-day window, so I'm not able to process a refund. I know that's not what you wanted to hear, happy to help with anything else on the account."

Reply 3 (easy — how-to question): "Hi Sam, you can update that from Account > Settings > Notifications, then just save at the bottom. Let me know if it doesn't stick."

Reply 4 (difficult — repeat complaint): "Hi Morgan, I see this is the second time you've reported this, I'm sorry it's still happening. I've escalated it directly to our engineering team with your account details so they can look deeper, and I'll personally follow up once I hear back."

Reply 5 (easy — thank you response): "That honestly makes our day, thank you for saying so! Passing this along to the team."

Reply 6 (difficult — angry customer, our error): "Hi Dana, you're right to be frustrated, we shipped the wrong size and that's on us. I've sent the correct one out today at no charge, no need to return the wrong item."

placeholders.name: PASTE 1-2, OR "none provided"
placeholders.what: One or two real replies your team agrees missed the mark, too stiff, too casual, over-apologetic, or otherwise off, so the AI can name specifically what went wrong instead of guessing. If you don't have an example handy, write "none provided" and skip this.
examples: "To Whom It May Concern, We regret to inform you that per our terms of service section 4.2, your request cannot be accommodated at this time. Regards, Customer Service Department" (too stiff/corporate)
"omg so sorry that happened to u!! that totally sucks lol, let me see what I can do" (too casual for the situation, a billing dispute)
"none provided"

variations.label: Comparing two agents' tone side by side
variations.whenToUse: Use when you want to understand how two specific agents' styles differ, before deciding what the team-wide standard should be.
variations.prompt:
I want to compare two agents' tone before deciding on a team-wide standard.

Agent A's replies: [PASTE 3-4 REAL REPLIES]
Agent B's replies: [PASTE 3-4 REAL REPLIES]

From these examples only: 1) describe the concrete, specific differences between how each agent writes (sentence length, how they open, how much they apologize, specific phrases), 2) note which specific patterns from each would be worth keeping in a team-wide standard, 3) don't declare one agent "better" overall, just describe the real differences and let me decide what to standardize on.

variations.label: Channel-specific tone guide (chat vs. email)
variations.whenToUse: Use when your team writes in more than one channel and the tone genuinely should differ, chat shorter and more casual, email more complete.
variations.prompt:
I want two versions of our tone guide, one for live chat, one for email, since the right tone genuinely differs by channel.

Real chat replies that hit our tone well: [PASTE 3-4 REAL CHAT REPLIES]
Real email replies that hit our tone well: [PASTE 3-4 REAL EMAIL REPLIES]

For each channel separately: 1) identify the concrete patterns (message length, formality, how greetings/sign-offs work, response speed expectations), 2) note the real differences between the two channels based on these examples, 3) give a short do's-and-don'ts list with an example for each, per channel. Do not invent a tone rule not reflected in the examples.

variations.label: Quick tone check on a single draft
variations.whenToUse: Use day-to-day once the guide exists, to check one specific draft against it without rebuilding the whole guide.
variations.prompt:
Check this draft reply against our team's tone guide before I send it.

Our tone guide: [PASTE YOUR TONE GUIDE OR ITS 5-POINT CHECKLIST]
My draft: [PASTE DRAFT]

Go through the checklist point by point and tell me where this draft passes or fails, with a specific fix for anything that fails, don't rewrite the whole thing, just flag and fix the specific issues.

followUps.label: Check no invented rule snuck in
followUps.prompt: Go through the guide point by point and confirm each do/don't is backed by a specific example from what I gave you. Flag anything that sounds like generic customer-service advice not actually reflected in my examples, and remove or revise it.

followUps.label: Make it more specific with real quotes
followUps.prompt: For each do/don't point, quote the exact sentence from my examples that demonstrates it, so the guide is anchored to real language, not just described in the abstract.

followUps.label: Checklist too long — cut to essentials
followUps.prompt: The pre-send checklist has too many points to realistically run through before sending every reply. Cut it to the 3 most important checks.

followUps.label: Add a weak example I forgot to include
followUps.prompt: I have another example that missed the mark: [PASTE EXAMPLE]. Add an analysis of specifically what's off about it, tied to a concrete pattern, and fold that into the existing guide.

cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.walkthrough:
Yuki manages a 6-person support team that's grown fast, and she's noticed replies vary a lot, one agent signs off formally with "Kind regards," another is almost too casual for a billing dispute. She wants a tone guide built from the team's own real writing, not generic advice nobody will actually reference.

She asks two teammates to nominate their best recent replies and pulls 5 real examples: an easy shipping update, a denied refund handled well, a repeat-complaint escalation, a thank-you response, and an apology for a shipping error that was genuinely their fault. She also has one example she saved months ago that was too corporate-sounding, opening with "To Whom It May Concern."

In ChatGPT, she pastes the lesson's prompt with all 5 good examples and the one weak one, labeled clearly. The AI identifies a real pattern: the good replies all state the answer or action in the first sentence before adding context, keep sentences short, and only apologize when the company was actually at fault. It flags the weak example specifically for its stiff corporate opening and lack of a direct answer. It produces a do's-and-don'ts guide with a quoted real example next to each point, plus a 5-point pre-send checklist.

Yuki reviews it and feels the checklist has too many items for agents to realistically run through before every send. She sends the follow-up: "Cut it to the 3 most important checks."

She shares the trimmed guide with the team in their next meeting.

Total time: about 30 minutes.

placeholders.name: LIST, e.g. "billing, shipping, technical, account access, general question, complaint/escalation"
placeholders.what: Your team's real, currently-used ticket categories exactly as they appear in your helpdesk system, don't invent new categories for this exercise.
examples: Billing, shipping, technical, account access, general question, complaint/escalation
Order issue, product question, returns/refunds, technical support, account/login, other
Bug report, feature request, billing, onboarding help, churn risk/cancellation

placeholders.name: LIST, e.g. "urgent, standard, low"
placeholders.what: The real priority levels your team currently uses to triage tickets, keep to your existing scale rather than introducing a new one.
examples: Urgent, standard, low
P1 (immediate), P2 (same day), P3 (this week)
Critical, high, normal, low

placeholders.name: LIST, e.g. "repeat contact within 48h, words like 'cancel'/'refund my money now', VIP account tag, angry tone"
placeholders.what: The actual real signals a human triager currently notices when judging urgency, specific words, repeat contact, account tier, tone. Naming these concretely is what lets the AI classification step approximate a real triager's judgment.
examples: Repeat contact within 48h, words like 'cancel' / 'refund my money now' / 'lawyer', VIP account tag, clearly angry tone, mentions of a competitor
Order marked as a gift with an upcoming event date mentioned, any mention of a safety issue, enterprise account tier
Multiple failed login attempts mentioned, any mention of unauthorized account access, phrases like 'I've been charged twice'

variations.label: Adding an AI-suggested reply step (after validation)
variations.whenToUse: Use only after the classification-only workflow has already run and been validated for a few weeks, this extends it to also suggest a reply, still requiring human send.
variations.prompt:
Our AI classification-and-routing workflow has been running and validated for [TIMEFRAME, e.g. "6 weeks"], with accuracy against past human decisions at [ACCURACY %]. I want to extend it to also draft a suggested reply, still requiring a human to review and send, never auto-sent.

Our real ticket categories: [LIST]
Our real priority levels: [LIST]
Signals we use: [LIST]

Design the addition: 1) what real data the AI reply-drafting step should use (ticket text, category, relevant macro from our library if one matches), 2) where the human review/send step sits, confirm it cannot be skipped, 3) which ticket categories or priority levels should be excluded from getting an AI-suggested reply at all, 4) the single biggest new risk this addition introduces.

variations.label: Smaller team — simplified single-queue version
variations.whenToUse: Use for a very small team (1-3 agents) where a full multi-queue routing system is overkill and a simpler priority-flag-only version makes more sense.
variations.prompt:
I run a small support team ([NUMBER] agents) and want a simplified version of an AI triage workflow, not full multi-queue routing, just an urgency flag to help me prioritize my own inbox.

Our real ticket categories: [LIST]
Our real priority levels: [LIST]
Signals we use to judge urgency: [LIST]

Design a simple version: 1) AI reads each incoming ticket and outputs just a priority flag + one-line reason, 2) low-confidence tickets get flagged for me to judge myself rather than guessed at, 3) which situations should always be flagged urgent regardless of AI confidence, 4) a lightweight way for me to spot-check accuracy weekly without a formal test setup.

variations.label: Designing the validation test in detail
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're ready to actually build the accuracy test against past tickets and need a detailed test plan, not just the high-level workflow design.
variations.prompt:
I'm ready to build the validation test for an AI ticket classification step before trusting it on live traffic.

Our real ticket categories: [LIST]
Our real priority levels: [LIST]
We have [NUMBER] real past tickets with known correct category/priority (what a human actually assigned).

Help me design the test in detail: 1) how to structure a spreadsheet or test set comparing AI classification to the known-correct human classification for each ticket, 2) what accuracy rate would be a reasonable bar before trusting it on live traffic for classification-only use, 3) how to break down accuracy by category so I know where to keep more human oversight even after rollout, 4) what to do about tickets where the AI was confident but wrong, specifically.

followUps.label: Tighten the always-human list
followUps.prompt: Review the always-human decision list again. Are there any other high-stakes situations specific to our business that should be added, anything involving money, legal exposure, safety, or a customer threatening to leave, that isn't already covered? Add any I'm missing.

followUps.label: Make the low-confidence rule concrete
followUps.prompt: The low-confidence-routes-to-human rule needs an actual threshold, not just a general principle. Suggest a specific, reasonable confidence threshold to start with, and explain how I'd adjust it up or down based on the first few weeks of real results.

followUps.label: Stress-test with an ambiguous example
followUps.prompt: Here's a real ambiguous ticket: [PASTE TICKET TEXT]. Walk through exactly how this workflow would classify and route it, step by step, and tell me whether it would correctly send this to a human or risk mishandling it.

followUps.label: Turn the test plan into a checklist
followUps.prompt: Turn the test plan into a concrete step-by-step checklist I can follow this week, including how many past tickets I need, what to record for each, and what result would mean I'm ready to roll out vs. need to adjust the workflow first.

cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.walkthrough:
Diego manages support for a growing SaaS company where ticket volume has outpaced his team's ability to manually read and route every incoming ticket before someone even starts working it. He wants AI to help with the first-pass sorting, but he's wary of anything auto-closing or auto-resolving a ticket without a human looking at it.

He opens his helpdesk platform's settings to confirm his team's real categories (billing, shipping, technical, account access, general question, complaint/escalation) and priority levels (urgent, standard, low), and writes down the real signals his senior agents currently use to judge urgency: repeat contact within 48 hours, specific words like "cancel" or "refund my money now," a VIP account tag, and clearly angry tone.

He pastes the lesson's prompt into Claude with those three lists filled in. The AI designs a workflow: ticket text and account metadata feed an AI classification step that outputs category, priority, and a confidence score; anything below a stated confidence threshold routes to a human review queue instead of being force-classified; an explicit always-human list covers anything mentioning cancellation or legal terms, any VIP account regardless of AI-assessed priority, and any auto-close action; and a test plan running the classifier against 100 recent resolved tickets, comparing results to what a human actually decided, before trusting it on live traffic.

Diego sends the follow-up asking it to stress-test the workflow against a real ambiguous ticket he has on hand, one where a frustrated customer mentions both a refund and canceling their account. The AI confirms this would correctly route to the human queue given the always-human list.

He builds the test set next, planning to run it before turning anything on live.

Total time: about 40 minutes.
